title: Diagnosis and Management of Trichomonas vaginalis: Summary of Evidence Reviewed for the 2021 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
article_subtype: Evidence review for the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines
medical_specialty: Infectious diseases and sexually transmitted infections
condition_or_topic: Diagnosis and management of Trichomonas vaginalis infection
clinical_background: Trichomonas vaginalis is likely the most prevalent nonviral sexually transmitted infection and is estimated to affect 3.7 million women and men in the United States. African Americans are >4 times more likely to have the infection than people of other races. Evidence published since the 2015 guidelines has strengthened links between infection in women and HIV acquisition, cervical cancer, preterm birth, and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, while its clinical significance in men remains less clear. New diagnostic tests and additional treatment evidence have prompted a reassessment of clinical care.
objectives: Review current evidence on the epidemiology, clinical significance, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of Trichomonas vaginalis infection to inform updates to the Trichomonas section of the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines.
study_design: Evidence review for the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines, based on a PubMed search, relevant conference abstracts, and additional unpublished data included with the authors’ permission. An expert committee reviewed the evidence, and 125 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis.

population.description: English-language research involving humans and addressing T. vaginalis epidemiology, diagnosis, or management.
inclusion_criteria: Relevant human-subject research published between 1 January 2013 and 1 December 2019.
Relevant articles published before 1 January 2013 (n = 80) or after 1 December 2019 (n = 4).
Relevant abstracts from STI conferences identified using the stated dates and search terms.
Additional unpublished data known to the expert committee, included with the authors’ permission.
exclusion_criteria: Articles unrelated to treatment or diagnosis (n=1299).

interpretation: The authors conclude that Trichomonas vaginalis is common, causes substantial reproductive morbidity in women and contributes to HIV transmission. Evidence linking infection to adverse obstetric outcomes has grown. In women, recent randomized trials indicate that a single oral 2 g dose of metronidazole is less effective than the twice-daily 7-day regimen. Diagnostic options have expanded, including highly sensitive and specific point-of-care tests, principally for women but also some for men.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier guidance preferred single-dose oral metronidazole for most patients. The preferred regimen changed to 7-day metronidazole for women with HIV after a randomized trial, but initially remained unchanged for women without HIV because that trial did not include them. A subsequent meta-analysis and multicenter randomized trial in women without HIV found that repeat infection was half as likely with the 7-day regimen as with the 2-g dose, supporting the change for all women. Earlier work associated T. vaginalis with HIV acquisition; a later meta-analysis of 19 studies found that infected persons were 1.5 times more likely to acquire HIV. Since the 2015 guidelines, 2 meta-analyses have added evidence of associations with adverse birth outcomes. A later study of 355 isolates found no association between TVV positivity and genital symptoms, unlike an earlier link between TVV2 and more severe symptoms. Prior studies raised concern about false-positive NAAT results from testing too soon after treatment; a subsequent study supported waiting until 3 weeks after treatment completion.
clinical_implications: Because repeat T. vaginalis infections are common and can have sequelae similar to those of initial infection, a positive test after treatment may reflect treatment failure, reinfection from an untreated or infected original partner, or infection from a new partner; these possibilities call for different approaches.

T. vaginalis is associated with increased HIV acquisition risk, while direct evidence that coinfection increases HIV transmission is less consistent. The authors suggest that controlling T. vaginalis may help reduce HIV transmission, particularly where infection is common.

Studies associate maternal T. vaginalis infection with low birth weight, preterm delivery and premature rupture of membranes; perinatal transmission is rare but can cause neonatal vaginal or respiratory infection.
In randomized trials, BV increased metronidazole treatment failure among women with HIV but not among women without HIV. The explanation for this difference remains uncertain.
A meta-analysis associated T. vaginalis with a 1.9-fold risk of cervical neoplasia, whereas evidence concerning prostate cancer remains inconclusive.

The authors note that in vitro 5-nitroimidazole resistance does not necessarily correspond to clinical treatment failure. They report that treatment selected after in vitro resistance testing cures >80% of resistant infections.
practice_implications: Use oral metronidazole for 7 days as the preferred regimen for all women with T. vaginalis, with 2 g tinidazole as an alternative. The single-dose oral 2 g metronidazole regimen should not be used in women.
For men with or exposed to T. vaginalis, retain single-dose 2 g oral metronidazole as the recommended regimen and 2 g tinidazole as an alternative until further evidence is available.

Test women seeking care for vaginal discharge. Annual screening can be considered for women receiving care in high-prevalence settings and for asymptomatic persons at high risk; screening decisions should take local T. vaginalis epidemiology into account. Testing can be considered for men with urethritis.

Do not routinely test or screen oral or rectal sites for T. vaginalis in women or men. Do not use an incidental liquid Pap test finding as a screening test, wet mount microscopy for men, or OSOM on male urine specimens.
Screen asymptomatic women with HIV for T. vaginalis, as recommended by the CDC.
Retest all persons with T. vaginalis 3 months after treatment because repeat infection is common. When retesting with NAATs, wait until 3 weeks after treatment completion to avoid testing too soon.

Treat the sexual partners of persons with T. vaginalis and consider presumptive partner treatment. Expedited partner therapy may have a role, although no partner-management intervention has been demonstrated to be superior for reducing reinfection.

For a lactating woman receiving metronidazole, interrupting breastfeeding during treatment and for 12–24 hours after the final dose reduces infant exposure. For tinidazole, interrupt breastfeeding during treatment and for 3 days after the final dose.

Refer patients with immediate-type hypersensitivity reactions to metronidazole to an allergist for desensitization. If desensitization cannot be performed or tolerated, consider treatment outside the 5-nitroimidazole class; consultation with an infectious disease expert may be useful.

If infection persists in a woman after the 7-day metronidazole regimen and both reinfection from an untreated partner and medication noncompliance have been excluded, send the isolate to the CDC for 5-nitroimidazole susceptibility testing. While results are pending, give 2 g metronidazole or tinidazole daily for 7 days.

If that high-dose 7-day regimen fails, the reported successful options are oral tinidazole 2–3 g daily in divided doses plus intravaginal tinidazole 500 mg twice daily, both for 14 days, or oral tinidazole 2–3 g daily in divided doses plus paromomycin 4 g of 6.25% intravaginal cream nightly, both for 14 days. Avoid single-dose 5-nitroimidazole therapy for persistent infection.

For a man still infected after single-dose 2 g oral metronidazole who has been reexposed to an untreated partner, give another single 2 g metronidazole dose. If he has not been reexposed, give metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days.
limitations: Evidence is insufficient to establish whether screening and treating asymptomatic trichomoniasis in high-prevalence settings or high-risk persons reduces adverse health events, disparities or the community burden of infection.

There is no comparable clinical trial establishing the preferred treatment regimen in men, and no data establish optimal treatment for male partners of women with metronidazole-resistant trichomoniasis.
Tinidazole has not been evaluated in pregnant women.
Solana has not been evaluated in men.
open_questions: The clinical significance of T. vaginalis in asymptomatic women and in men remains insufficiently understood.
Whether T. vaginalis affects HIV transmission in the era of HIV preexposure prophylaxis requires further study.
It remains unclear whether BV interferes with T. vaginalis treatment outside the reported trial findings.
The association between T. vaginalis and prostate cancer remains inconclusive.
It is uncertain whether tinidazole is a better treatment than metronidazole for men.
future_directions: Conduct further treatment studies in men, including studies relevant to male partners of women with metronidazole-resistant infection.
Investigate the significance of infection in asymptomatic women and in men.
Study the influence of T. vaginalis on HIV transmission in the era of HIV preexposure prophylaxis.
Obtain additional evidence on the possible association with prostate cancer and on whether screening and treatment of asymptomatic infection reduce adverse outcomes.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that Trichomonas vaginalis is common and contributes to reproductive morbidity in women and HIV transmission, with growing evidence linking it to adverse obstetric outcomes. For women, the 7-day twice-daily metronidazole regimen is more effective than a single 2 g oral dose, which should no longer be used; diagnostic options have expanded, while infection in asymptomatic women and men warrants further study.
narrative_summary: This review assessed evidence on the epidemiology, clinical consequences, diagnosis, and management of Trichomonas vaginalis to inform the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines. The authors searched PubMed for English-language human research published from 1 January 2013 to 1 December 2019, considered additional relevant reports, and included 125 studies in the qualitative synthesis. The infection is frequently asymptomatic: 85% of women and 77% of men with T. vaginalis have no symptoms. The review describes associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes and increased HIV acquisition; a cited meta-analysis of 19 studies found that people with T. vaginalis were 1.5 times more likely to acquire HIV. NAATs offer the greatest diagnostic sensitivity, whereas wet mount microscopy has a sensitivity of 44%–68% compared with NAATs. Diagnostic testing is recommended for women presenting with vaginal discharge, and screening of asymptomatic women with HIV is recommended. Evidence from a meta-analysis and a multicenter randomized trial supports 7-day oral metronidazole rather than a single 2 g dose for women; the single-dose regimen remains recommended for men because a comparable trial in men is lacking. Repeat infection is common, and retesting 3 months after treatment remains recommended. The authors note that more research is needed on asymptomatic infection in women and the clinical significance of infection in men.

main_findings.description: The review describes T. vaginalis as likely the most prevalent nonviral sexually transmitted infection worldwide.
main_findings.context: Global estimate among women; its estimated prevalence exceeds that of Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and syphilis combined.

main_findings.description: A US population-based study using urine NAATs found T. vaginalis infection in women.
main_findings.context: Women in the US population-based study.

main_findings.description: The same US population-based study found T. vaginalis infection in men.
main_findings.context: Men in the US population-based study.

main_findings.description: The estimated annual number of new T. vaginalis infections in the US is substantial.
main_findings.context: US estimate.

main_findings.description: A US population-based study found substantially greater T. vaginalis prevalence among African Americans than among other racial groups.
main_findings.context: Risk factors reported by the study also included female sex, older age, 2 or more sexual partners in the past year, less than a high school education, poverty, and a history of incarceration.

main_findings.description: A study of T. vaginalis isolates found no association between TVV positivity and genital symptoms.
main_findings.context: Study of 355 T. vaginalis isolates; this contrasts with an earlier reported link between TVV2 and more severe genital symptoms.

main_findings.description: Most women with T. vaginalis infection have no symptoms.
main_findings.context: Women with T. vaginalis infection.

main_findings.description: Most men with T. vaginalis infection have no symptoms.
main_findings.context: Men with T. vaginalis infection.

main_findings.description: Some initially asymptomatic women may develop symptoms during follow-up.
main_findings.context: Initially asymptomatic women; within 6 months.

main_findings.description: The article reports a higher vaginal pH during some T. vaginalis infections, while noting that infection can also occur at normal pH.
main_findings.context: Normal vaginal pH is reported as 4.5.

main_findings.description: Colpitis macularis is identified less often on pelvic examination than with colposcopy.
main_findings.context: Women examined by pelvic examination; detection with colposcopy rises to nearly 50%.

main_findings.description: Two meta-analyses published since the earlier guidelines strengthened the reported association of maternal T. vaginalis with adverse birth outcomes.
main_findings.context: Reported outcomes included low birth weight, preterm delivery, and premature rupture of membranes.

main_findings.description: A meta-analysis found greater HIV acquisition among people with T. vaginalis.
main_findings.context: Meta-analysis of 19 peer-reviewed studies; comparison was with people without T. vaginalis.

main_findings.description: A review found that some studies reported greater genital-fluid HIV shedding in people with both HIV and T. vaginalis than in people with HIV without Trichomonas infection.
main_findings.context: Evidence for an effect on HIV transmission was described as less direct.

main_findings.description: A published model attributed a substantial share of HIV infections to T. vaginalis in a community where T. vaginalis was common.
main_findings.context: Estimate by Sorvillo and Kerndt for a high-prevalence community, not a directly observed effect.

main_findings.description: Another published model estimated the share of HIV infections among US women attributable to T. vaginalis.
main_findings.context: Estimate by Chesson et al; no newer models were reported since the 2015 guidelines.

main_findings.description: Co-occurrence of BV was reported among women with T. vaginalis.
main_findings.context: Women with T. vaginalis; the article also reports greater T. vaginalis acquisition risk among women with BV.

main_findings.description: A study in Tanzania found high-risk HPV more likely among women with T. vaginalis.
main_findings.context: Study of women in Tanzania; the authors describe this as suggesting an indirect connection with cervical neoplasia.

main_findings.description: A meta-analysis associated T. vaginalis with cervical neoplasia.
main_findings.context: Association reported by a cited meta-analysis.

main_findings.description: Studies in several countries found elevated odds of cervical neoplasia among women with T. vaginalis, or the reverse association.
main_findings.context: Studies of Finnish, Dutch, Belgian, and Chinese women; the direction of the association varied as stated.

main_findings.description: Whether T. vaginalis is associated with prostate cancer remains unresolved.
main_findings.context: The article states that further evidence is needed.

main_findings.description: Wet mount microscopy was less sensitive than NAATs for T. vaginalis.
main_findings.context: Testing in women; performance depends on reader expertise. Sensitivity decreases to 20% within 1 hour after collection, so the slide should be read within 10 minutes.

main_findings.description: A cited comparison found culture more sensitive than wet mount relative to polymerase chain reaction.
main_findings.context: Culture versus wet mount, respectively; culture was also described as slower, more expensive, and poorly sensitive in men.

main_findings.description: A cited randomized trial among women without HIV found fewer positive tests of cure after multidose metronidazole than after single-dose treatment.
main_findings.metric: proportion with T. vaginalis at test of cure
main_findings.context: metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days versus single-dose 2 g; test of cure at 1 month. The article supplies no arm-specific proportions.

main_findings.description: A cited meta-analysis and multicenter randomized trial found fewer repeat infections in women without HIV receiving the longer metronidazole regimen.
main_findings.context: 7-day regimen versus the 2-g dose; the article consequently identifies the 7-day oral metronidazole regimen as preferred for all women.

main_findings.description: A cited phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled study found secnidazole more effective than placebo for trichomoniasis.
main_findings.context: Women received a single 2-g oral dose; no numerical treatment-effect estimate is provided.

main_findings.description: Repeat T. vaginalis infections were common across the cited evidence.
main_findings.context: Reported range across studies; potential explanations include treatment failure, reinfection from a baseline partner, and infection from a new partner.

main_findings.description: US isolate studies found generally low in vitro metronidazole resistance.
main_findings.context: Studies involved mostly women without HIV; resistance was usually resolved with another course of metronidazole at the same or a higher dose.

main_findings.description: The review reports a range of in vitro resistance rates for approved 5-nitroimidazole drugs.
main_findings.context: No new resistance studies were identified in the review. In vitro resistance may not correspond precisely to clinical failure.

main_findings.description: Recommended alternative regimens selected after in vitro resistance testing were associated with cure of most resistant infections.
main_findings.context: Resistant T. vaginalis infections; this was presented as support for resistance testing.

main_findings.description: A cited randomized trial found a substantial reduction in repeat infection among women when partners received tinidazole.
main_findings.context: Partner treatment with 2 g tinidazole; 2 other studies of 2 g metronidazole for male partners reported either no effect or a borderline effect.

notable_adverse_events: Reported reactions to metronidazole include urticaria and facial edema; other reported immediate-type hypersensitivity reactions include flushing, fever, and anaphylactic shock. No rates are provided.
Intravaginal paromomycin cream may cause vaginal ulceration, which can resolve spontaneously after treatment stops. No rate is provided.
Several cited meta-analyses found metronidazole safe throughout pregnancy; tinidazole had not been evaluated in pregnant women. No adverse-event rates are provided.

subgroup_analyses: In a cited randomized trial of women with HIV and T. vaginalis, 7-day metronidazole outperformed single-dose treatment. A subsequent analysis found that this superiority occurred only when BV was present; the article provides no subgroup effect estimates.
Cited randomized trials found that BV increased metronidazole treatment failure among women with HIV but not among women without HIV. The proposed reasons for this difference remain uncertain.

Cited cohorts of women with HIV in Kenya and New Orleans observed less vaginal HIV shedding after T. vaginalis treatment; the cohorts used different diagnostic methods, and no numerical effect estimates are provided.
For women, the laboratory-test table reports Culture sensitivity of 75%–96% and specificity of 100%; for men, sensitivity is 50%–80% and specificity is 100%.
For women, the laboratory-test table reports Hologic Aptima T. vaginalis assay sensitivity of 88%–100% and specificity of 98%–100%.
For women, the laboratory-test table reports BD Max CT/GC/TV2 assay sensitivity of 89.8%–99.7% and specificity of 98.1%–99.5%; for men, sensitivity is 81.1%–100% and specificity is 98.7%–100%.

For women, the laboratory-test table reports Roche Cobas TV/MG assay sensitivity of 96.4%–100% and specificity of 96.5%–98.8%; for men, sensitivity is 77.2%–100% and specificity is 97.2%–99.9%. The prose gives a different overall specificity range.

For symptomatic women, the point-of-care table reports OSOM sensitivity of 83%–92% and specificity of 99%–100%; for asymptomatic or symptomatic women, Solana sensitivity is 90%–99% and specificity is 97%–99%, and AmpliVue sensitivity is 97%–100% and specificity is 97%–99%.
For women, the point-of-care table reports Cepheid GeneXpert sensitivity of 95%–100% and specificity of 98%–99%; no separate male performance estimate appears in that table.
secondary_results: T. vaginalis mainly infects genital squamous epithelium. Infection may last months or years in women but may be shorter in men, for example less than a month.

Extragenital oral or rectal T. vaginalis infection is described as occasional and much less frequent than genital infection. Infection is also described as very uncommon among men who have sex with men.

In the cited clinical evidence, symptomatic women could have vaginal erythema, dyspareunia, dysuria, vaginal discharge, or genital pruritus; reported complications included Skene and Bartholin gland infections and increased pelvic inflammatory disease risk among women with HIV. In men, reported manifestations included urethritis, epididymitis, prostatitis, and reduced sperm motility.

A single cited study associated maternal T. vaginalis infection with intellectual disability in children, but the article reports no additional studies of that outcome. Rare perinatal transmission can cause neonatal vaginal or respiratory infection.

T. vaginalis was associated in cited studies with HSV-2 shedding, increased HSV-2 incidence among infected women, and the presence of other sexually transmitted infections, including C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and HPV.

Culture failed to detect some infections in longitudinal studies of women with and without HIV: after single-dose metronidazole, infection was undetectable by culture for months and later reappeared without reported sexual exposure.
The article reports that liquid Pap testing can identify T. vaginalis incidentally but is not reliable for diagnosis or screening.

A cited study supported waiting 3 weeks after completion of treatment before retesting with NAATs to reduce false-positive results from testing too soon. Retesting at 3 months after treatment remains recommended because repeat infection is common.

For women with persistent infection after 7-day metronidazole, once partner reinfection and nonadherence have been ruled out, the article describes CDC susceptibility testing and 2 g metronidazole or tinidazole daily for 7 days while results are pending. It reports successful additional options after failure of that high-dose course but supplies no response proportions for those options.

The article reports occasional treatment success with intravaginal boric acid 600 mg twice daily for 60 days or intravaginal paromomycin 6.25% cream nightly for 14 days when desensitization cannot be performed or tolerated. It cautions that these treatments may not reach all infected sites.
Nitazoxanide was investigated for metronidazole-resistant T. vaginalis but was not found effective. Plant extracts showed anti–T. vaginalis activity but had not been tested in clinical trials.

A cited estimate projected that following the CDC screening and treatment recommendation for women with HIV would avert new HIV infections with lifetime costs of approximately US$159 264 000, through prevention of cases arising from female-to-male transmission; this is a modeled estimate, not an observed trial result.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: Trichomonas vaginalis is probably the most prevalent nonviral sexually transmitted infection and affects an estimated 3.7 million women and men in the United States. African Americans are >4 times more likely to have the infection than people of other races. Evidence published since the 2015 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines has strengthened associations between infection in women and HIV acquisition, cervical cancer, preterm birth, and other adverse pregnancy outcomes; its clinical importance in men is less well understood. New point-of-care assays and nucleic acid amplification tests permit more accurate, convenient testing of several genital specimen types, including urine. Repeat or persistent infection is common in women, supporting rescreening at 3 months after treatment. In vitro resistance to 5-nitroimidazole remains low (4.3%) but warrants monitoring. Frequent infection among sexual partners suggests a possible role for expedited partner treatment. In a randomized trial involving women without HIV, metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days resulted in a lower proportion with infection at the 1 month test of cure than a single 2 g dose. A single oral 2-g dose of metronidazole remains the preferred treatment for men.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Trichomonas vaginalis is a prevalent parasite that causes the sexually transmitted infection trichomoniasis. Since the literature review conducted in 2013 for the 2015 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention treatment guidelines, further evidence has appeared on its epidemiology, clinical consequences, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment. This article reviews evidence in those areas used to update the Trichomonas section of the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: An expert committee developed questions and an evidence table concerning updates to trichomoniasis epidemiology, diagnosis, and management for the 2021 CDC STI treatment guidelines. PubMed was searched for English-language human research on T. vaginalis published between 1 January 2013 and 1 December 2019. Searches for “trichomonas,” “Trichomonas vaginalis,” and “trichomoniasis” yielded 1590 articles, 1102 articles, and 594 articles, respectively. Relevant publications from before 1 January 2013 (n = 80) and after 1 December 2019 (n = 4) were also included. Relevant conference abstracts, both printed and online, were reviewed using the same dates and terms. The search yielded 1676 nonduplicated papers. Reviewers examined every abstract and the full text of pertinent articles for information relevant to the 2021 guidelines. With author permission, the committee also added unpublished information known to it to the evidence tables. Evidence quality was discussed by the committee and at the CDC STI Treatment Guidelines Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, on 11–13 June 2019. The study-selection diagram reports 3286 database records, 1676 records after duplicate removal, 1676 screened records, 1676 full texts assessed, 1551 full texts excluded, and 125 studies included in qualitative synthesis. Its exclusion categories are review papers (n =249), non-human studies (n=3), and papers unrelated to treatment or diagnosis (n=1299).

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The following subsections review evidence on epidemiology and clinical effects, diagnostic approaches, treatment, repeat infection, partner management, and antimicrobial resistance.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology and Clinical Significance of T. vaginalis
document_sections.content: Trichomonas vaginalis is probably the world's most frequent nonviral STI. Although reporting is not mandatory, estimates indicate 156 million new infections annually among women worldwide; its global prevalence exceeds the combined prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and syphilis. A recent US population-based study using urine NAATs reported prevalence of 1.8% in women and 0.5% in men, while an estimated 3.1 million new US infections occur each year. African Americans had a >4-fold higher prevalence than other racial groups. Other reported risk factors were female sex, older age, 2 or more sexual partners during the preceding year, less than a high school education, poverty, and prior incarceration. Prevalence is very low among men who have sex with men. Oral or rectal infection occurs occasionally but is far less common than genital infection; oral and rectal testing or screening is therefore not currently recommended for women or men. The extracellular parasite chiefly infects genital squamous epithelium: the vagina, urethra, and endocervix in women, and the urethra and prostate in men. Humans are its only known host, and sexual intercourse is its principal route of transmission. Infection can persist for months or possibly years in women but may last less than a month in men. The parasite apparently lacks a cyst form and survives poorly outside the body, although survival in warm, wet conditions for >3 hours has been reported. A possible pseudocyst form is more virulent in animals and might matter in humans, particularly for cervical neoplasia. Transmission through fomites and possibly water is considered rare but has been described. T. vaginalis can carry 1 of 4 dsRNA viruses collectively called T. vaginalis virus (TVV); earlier research linked TVV2 to more severe genital symptoms. In contrast, a subsequent study of 355 isolates found TVV in 40% and no association between TVV positivity and genital symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Presentation of T. vaginalis
document_sections.content: Most infected women (85%) and men (77%) have no symptoms. Half of initially asymptomatic women may develop symptoms within 6 months. Symptomatic women may have vaginal erythema, dyspareunia, dysuria, genital pruritus, and discharge that is often widespread, malodorous, and yellow-green. Vaginal pH, normally 4.5, often rises to >5 during infection, although infection can occur with a normal pH. Colpitis macularis, also called “strawberry cervix,” is observed in about 5% of women during pelvic examination and nearly 50% during colposcopy. Reported complications in women include Skene and Bartholin gland infection and, among women with HIV, increased pelvic inflammatory disease risk. In men, infection can cause urethritis, epididymitis, prostatitis, and reduced sperm motility.

document_sections.heading: T. vaginalis and Perinatal Outcomes
document_sections.content: Since the 2015 guidelines, 2 published meta-analyses have added evidence linking T. vaginalis to low birth weight, preterm delivery, and premature rupture of membranes. One study associated maternal infection with intellectual disability in children born to infected mothers, but no further studies of that outcome have appeared. Perinatal transmission is uncommon but can cause vaginal or respiratory infection in neonates.

document_sections.heading: T. vaginalis and HIV Transmission
document_sections.content: Earlier investigations associated T. vaginalis with greater HIV acquisition risk. A meta-analysis of 19 peer-reviewed studies published since the 2015 guidelines found that people with T. vaginalis were 1.5 times more likely to acquire HIV. Proposed biological explanations are recruitment of HIV target cells to inflamed genital mucosa, disruption of the mucosal barrier through punctate hemorrhages, and changes in vaginal microbiota that favor bacterial vaginosis (BV), which can itself raise HIV acquisition risk. The effect on HIV transmission in the era of HIV preexposure prophylaxis requires further study. Direct evidence that people with both infections transmit HIV more often is weaker: a review found increased genital HIV shedding in 7 of 14 studies comparing people with T. vaginalis against those with HIV but without Trichomonas infection. HIV vaginal shedding decreased after T. vaginalis treatment in separate cohorts of Kenyan women diagnosed by microscopy and culture and women in New Orleans diagnosed by culture. Sorvillo and Kerndt estimated that up to 20% of HIV infections in a community with high T. vaginalis prevalence could be attributable to the parasite. Chesson et al estimated an attributable proportion of 6.2% among all HIV infections in US women. No newer models have appeared since the 2015 guidelines. Controlling T. vaginalis might therefore be a cost-effective means of reducing HIV transmission where the parasite is common or in groups with higher prevalence, including African Americans. Although those studies preceded consideration of HIV treatment as prevention, they support the importance of screening and treating women at risk of trichomoniasis.

document_sections.heading: T. vaginalis and Other STIs
document_sections.content: T. vaginalis appears to have a bidirectional epidemiologic relationship with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). Coinfection has been associated with HSV-2 shedding, and women with T. vaginalis have had higher HSV-2 incidence. Associations have also been reported with C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and human papillomavirus (HPV).

document_sections.heading: T. vaginalis and Bacterial Vaginosis
document_sections.content: BV occurs in up to 40%–60% of women with T. vaginalis, while women with BV have increased risk of acquiring T. vaginalis. Vaginal dysbiosis has been associated with greater T. vaginalis pathogenicity, but whether BV impairs its treatment remains uncertain. In randomized trials, BV increased metronidazole treatment failure among women with HIV but not among women without HIV. Possible explanations for this difference include impaired immunity in women with HIV, altered metronidazole pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics, and inadequate study power.

document_sections.heading: T. vaginalis and Neoplasia
document_sections.content: A Tanzanian study published since the 2015 guidelines found that women with T. vaginalis were 6.5 times more likely to have high-risk HPV, suggesting a possible indirect connection with cervical neoplasia. A meta-analysis associated T. vaginalis with a 1.9-fold risk of cervical neoplasia. Studies involving Finnish, Dutch, Belgian, and Chinese women reported elevated odds (1.4–2.0) of cervical neoplasia among women with T. vaginalis or the converse. Evidence concerning an association with prostate cancer remains inconclusive, and more data are needed.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostics
document_sections.content: Women presenting for care because of vaginal discharge should undergo T. vaginalis testing. Annual screening can be considered for women receiving care in high-prevalence settings, such as STD clinics or correctional facilities, and for asymptomatic people at high risk, including those with multiple sexual partners, exchange of sex for payment, illicit drug use, or a history of STD or incarceration. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether screening and treating asymptomatic infection in these settings or groups reduces adverse outcomes, health disparities, or community infection burden. Although population-based prevalence in men is low (0.5%), testing can be considered for men with urethritis. Local epidemiology should inform screening decisions. Diagnostic options have expanded and become more precise since the 2015 guidelines. Wet mount microscopy is inexpensive and usable at the point of care in women but has sensitivity of 44%–68% relative to NAATs, varies with reader expertise, and is not recommended for men. Slides should be examined within 10 minutes of collection because sensitivity falls rapidly, reaching 20% within 1 hour. Compared with polymerase chain reaction, culture is more sensitive than wet mount (66% vs 48%) but costs more, takes longer, and performs poorly in men. In separate longitudinal studies of women without and with HIV, infection became undetectable by culture for months after single-dose metronidazole and then reappeared despite no reported sexual exposure, illustrating that culture can miss infection. An incidental finding on a liquid Pap test is unreliable for diagnosis and should not be used for screening. FDA-approved BD Affirm VPIII detects T. vaginalis, Gardnerella, and Candida species in vaginal fluid; reported sensitivity is 91%–100%, specificity 93%–96%, and result time <1 hour. NAATs are the most sensitive tests and are moderately priced but technically complex. Aptima T. vaginalis assay, cleared by the FDA in 2011 for specified urine, swab, and Hologic PreserveCyt solution (ThinPrep) specimens from symptomatic and asymptomatic women, has sensitivity and specificity of 95%–100%; use in men requires internal validation under CLIA because FDA clearance does not cover men. BD Probe Tec TV Qx Amplified DNA Assay is FDA-cleared for specified vaginal, endocervical, and urine specimens from women; compared with wet mount and culture, sensitivity is 98.3% and specificity 99.6%. Its use in men likewise requires internal CLIA validation. The same specimen may be used for these NAATs and chlamydia or gonorrhea screening, but screening for the latter infections is chiefly recommended for sexually active women aged 24 years and younger, whereas trichomoniasis is more common in women >24 years; this older group should not be overlooked. FDA-cleared BD Max CTGCTV2 assay accepts specified vaginal specimens and urine from women and men, with sensitivity ranging from 81.1% to 100% and specificity from 98.7% to 100%, depending on specimen type. Roche Cobas TV/MG test accepts specified vaginal and endocervical specimens from women and urine and meatal swabs from men; sensitivity is 77.2%–100% and specificity 96.1%–99.9%. Table 1 summarizes laboratory-based tests by specimen, diagnostic performance, complexity, turnaround time, and cost. Other FDA-cleared point-of-care options for women include OSOM, Isothermal Helicase-Dependent AmpliVue, and Solana TV assay. Cepheid GeneXpert TV assay is a moderately complex rapid test completed in <1 hour and cleared for specified female urine, endocervical, and vaginal specimens and male urine. Its reported sensitivities and specificities range from 99.5% to 100% and 99.4% to 99.9%, respectively, against wet mount and culture. In women, these rapid tests have sensitivity and specificity >97%, but generally cost more than standard NAATs on high-volume platforms. OSOM is unsuitable for male urine because its sensitivity is 37.5%; Solana has not been evaluated in men. Table 2 summarizes point-of-care tests by specimen, performance, complexity, turnaround time, and cost.

document_sections.heading: Treatment of T. vaginalis Infection
document_sections.content: Previously, CDC and the World Health Organization favored a single oral 2 g metronidazole dose, with oral metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 7 days or oral tinidazole 2 g as alternatives. Both drugs are 5-nitroimidazoles. Following a multicenter RCT that found 7-day metronidazole superior to a single dose in women with HIV, the 2015 guidelines made the 7-day regimen preferred for that group, with 2 g tinidazole as an alternative. The preference was not extended to women without HIV at that time because the trial involved only women with HIV. Since then, a meta-analysis and a multicenter RCT have found similar results in women without HIV: repeat infection was half as likely with the 7-day regimen as with the 2-g dose. Accordingly, oral metronidazole for 7 days is now preferred for all women, with 2 g tinidazole as an alternative; single-dose 2-g metronidazole is no longer recommended for women. In the absence of a comparable trial in men, metronidazole 2 g remains recommended for men who have T. vaginalis or were exposed to it, with tinidazole 2 g as an alternative pending further research. Oral secnidazole is a newer 5-nitroimidazole with a longer half-life (~17 hours) than metronidazole (~7–8 hours) or tinidazole (~12–13 hours). It was FDA-approved for BV and was emerging as a trichomoniasis option for women. A phase 3 multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, delayed-treatment, double-blind study found a single oral 2-g secnidazole dose superior to placebo for trichomoniasis. If FDA-approved for this indication, it would be the only oral single-dose drug for both BV and T. vaginalis.

document_sections.heading: Treatment for Pregnant and Lactating Women
document_sections.content: Metronidazole is classified as class B, and several meta-analyses have found it safe throughout pregnancy. Tinidazole has not been evaluated in pregnant women and remains class C. For lactating women receiving metronidazole, stopping breastfeeding during treatment and for 12–24 hours after the final dose reduces infant exposure. For those receiving tinidazole, interruption during treatment and for 3 days after the final dose is recommended.

document_sections.heading: Approach to Determining if Infection Posttreatment Is a Repeat or Persistent Infection
document_sections.content: Repeat T. vaginalis infection occurs in 5% to 37% of cases and has consequences similar to those of initial infection. A positive posttreatment test may reflect treatment failure, reinfection by an untreated or infected original partner, or acquisition from a new partner. These possibilities require different responses to prevent continuing infection. Reinfection calls for ensuring treatment of the original partners, potentially through expedited partner treatment; suspected treatment failure calls for further testing followed by appropriate treatment. The accompanying figure presents approaches to infection detected again after treatment. US in vitro studies have consistently found low metronidazole resistance. Reported resistance among predominantly women without HIV ranges from 2.2% to 9.6% and was generally resolved by another metronidazole course at the same or a higher dose. Most recurrent infections are probably reinfections. Nevertheless, among women treated with a single 2-g metronidazole dose, treatment failure was the most likely explanation for a subsequent positive test. Failure rates may fall as 7-day metronidazole becomes more widely used.

document_sections.heading: Rescreening
document_sections.content: The recommendation to retest all people with T. vaginalis 3 months after treatment remains in place because repeat infection is frequent. The earliest suitable retesting time has changed: prior studies showed that NAAT retesting too soon can produce false-positive results, and an additional study published since 2015 supported 3 weeks after treatment completion as the optimal earliest NAAT retesting time.

document_sections.heading: Treatment for Persons With 5-Nitroimidazole Allergies or Persistent T. vaginalis
document_sections.content: The most commonly reported metronidazole reactions are urticaria and facial edema; flushing, fever, and anaphylactic shock can also result from immediate immunoglobulin E–mediated hypersensitivity. Referral to an allergist for desensitization is advised in these circumstances. If desensitization cannot be undertaken or tolerated, agents outside the 5-nitroimidazole class should be considered. Regimens including intravaginal boric acid 600 mg twice daily for 60 days and intravaginal paromomycin 6.25% cream nightly for 14 days have occasionally succeeded in women. They may fail to reach infected Bartholin or Skene glands, require compounding, cost more, and may cause adverse effects. Paromomycin cream can cause vaginal ulceration that may resolve spontaneously after treatment stops. Consultation with an infectious disease expert may help. If infection persists in a woman after 7-day multidose metronidazole and both reinfection from an untreated partner and medication noncompliance have been excluded, her isolate should be sent to CDC for 5-nitroimidazole susceptibility testing. While results are pending, metronidazole or tinidazole 2 g daily for 7 days should be given. If this high-dose 7-day oral course fails, 2 regimens have been successful: oral tinidazole 2–3 g daily in divided doses plus intravaginal tinidazole 500 mg twice daily, both for 14 days; or oral tinidazole 2–3 g daily in divided doses plus paromomycin 4 g of 6.25% intravaginal cream nightly, both for 14 days. Single-dose 5-nitroimidazole treatment should be avoided in persistent infection. Intravaginal acetarsol, boric acid, and furazolidone have been studied or remain under investigation for resistant infection but are not commonly used. Oral nitazoxanide was investigated for metronidazole-resistant infection and was not effective. Plant extracts have shown anti–T. vaginalis activity but have not undergone clinical trials. A man still infected after a single oral metronidazole 2 g dose who was reexposed to an untreated partner should receive another single 2 g dose. Without reexposure, he should receive metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. No data currently establish optimal treatment for male partners of women with metronidazole-resistant trichomoniasis.

document_sections.heading: Treatment for Women With HIV Infection
document_sections.content: A randomized trial in women with HIV and T. vaginalis found 7-day metronidazole superior to single-dose treatment. Subsequent analysis found superiority only when BV was present. The authors suggest that some BV-associated organisms might absorb metronidazole. Studies have also suggested that protease inhibitors used for HIV may impair metronidazole effectiveness in women with HIV. Because T. vaginalis rates are high in women with HIV and treatment can reduce vaginal HIV shedding, CDC recommends screening asymptomatic women with HIV for T. vaginalis. One estimate projected that following the CDC screening and treatment recommendation for these women would yield approximately US$159 264 000 in lifetime costs of new HIV infections averted through prevention of female-to-male transmission.

document_sections.heading: Partner Management
document_sections.content: Sexual partners of people with T. vaginalis should receive treatment. Patients are commonly asked to advise partners to seek testing and treatment, while providers should consider presumptive partner treatment. Expedited partner therapy may help, but no partner-management intervention has been shown superior for reducing reinfection. One randomized clinical trial found that treating partners with tinidazole 2 g reduced repeat infection among women with T. vaginalis by >4-fold. Two other studies that gave male partners metronidazole 2 g found either no effect or a borderline effect of expedited treatment. Those metronidazole studies may have lacked power or appropriate controls; tinidazole might also be more effective in men. More treatment studies in men are needed.

document_sections.heading: Antimicrobial Resistance
document_sections.content: Currently approved drugs are 5-nitroimidazoles, including metronidazole and tinidazole. In vitro resistance rates range from 4.3% to 10%, and this review identified no new resistance studies. Laboratory resistance does not necessarily correspond exactly to clinical failure, particularly in pregnant women. Nevertheless, recommended alternative regimens selected after in vitro resistance testing cure >80% of resistant infections, suggesting value in such testing.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: T. vaginalis is highly prevalent, causes substantial reproductive morbidity in women, and contributes to HIV transmission. Evidence increasingly links it to poor obstetrical outcomes. Treatment recommendations have changed because recent randomized clinical trials found the formerly preferred single oral metronidazole 2 g dose less effective for women than twice-daily treatment for 7 days; the single dose should not be used in women. Diagnostic options have expanded markedly, including highly sensitive and specific point-of-care tests, mostly for women but also some for men. The clinical significance of infection in asymptomatic women and in men needs further investigation.
